name: El Nido Airport
before:
A small airstrip serving El Nido in Palawan, about 4 km from the town proper in the barangay of Villa Libertad.

The ownership is unusual and worth knowing. The airport is owned and operated by Cebu Pacific rather than by a public authority, so the schedule is effectively one airline's decision. Check what is flying before promising a client a date.

It is also known as Lio Airport, so both names appear in supplier systems.

There is a single concrete airstrip. An older gravel runway is now partly surfaced and used as a taxiway.
after:
A small airstrip serving El Nido in Palawan, about 4 km from the town proper.

The airline side has changed and is worth knowing. AirSWIFT, the boutique airline that has long flown here, now belongs to Cebu Pacific. From 1 July 2026 its flights are run by Cebgo, Cebu Pacific's turboprop airline, under DG flight numbers instead of T6. Check what is flying before promising a client a date.

It is also known as Lio Airport.

There is a single concrete airstrip.

claims.claim: owned and operated by Cebu Pacific, not a public authority
claims.wasBefore: The airport is owned and operated by Cebu Pacific rather than by a public authority
claims.why: Not confirmed, and Wikipedia contradicts itself: its text says the airstrip is owned and operated by Cebu Pacific, its infobox gives the owner as Cebu Pacific but the operator as Ten Knots Development Corp. No second source on the airport's owner or operator could be read: AirSWIFT's own site (www.air-swift.com) does not resolve; CAAP's aerodrome certification list of 10 September 2026 covers only four certified aerodromes (Manila, Puerto Princesa, Bohol-Panglao, Kalibo) and is a scanned image; the provincial government's site has no airport page and its tourism site (turismo.palawan.gov.ph) does not resolve; AvGeek and Inquirer Insider report the airline deal, not the airport; BusinessWorld's tag page timed out and Ayala Land's news index shows only current items. What two sources do confirm is that Cebu Pacific owns the airline that flies here (see above).

claims.claim: Manila flights moved to Clark on 29 March 2026; current routes
claims.why: Held back: a verified new fact that replaces nothing, and the one most likely to catch a UK traveller out, for Andy to add if he wants. From 29 March 2026 AirSWIFT's daily flights between Manila and El Nido became Clark to El Nido flights, under the government's order moving turboprops out of Manila's NAIA (AvGeek, January 2026). By June 2026 both AvGeek and Inquirer Insider list El Nido's routes as Clark, Boracay, Bohol, Cebu and Coron, with no Manila route. So a client arriving in Manila would need to get to Clark, or connect another way (for example through Cebu). AvGeek's June piece still calls Clark 'an alternative gateway', loose wording given its own January report and its route list.

quote: Affected routes include multiple daily flights between Manila and El Nido, which will be re-designated as Clark–El Nido–Clark services.
The move, which will take effect on 29 March 2026
Cebu Pacific said affected passengers will be automatically transferred to a new flight departing from Clark.

sources.quote: AirSWIFT operates routes linking Clark and El Nido, as well as flights connecting El Nido with Boracay, Bohol, Cebu and Coron.

claims.claim: FCDO: no advice against travel to Palawan; typhoon season
claims.why: Held back: the FCDO's current advice (updated 15 July 2026, still current 24 September 2026) replaces nothing in the old text. It advises against all travel to western and central Mindanao and the Sulu archipelago, and against all but essential travel to the rest of Mindanao except Camiguin, Dinagat and Siargao; nothing covers Palawan. It notes around 20 typhoons a year, most between June and November, which matters for small turboprops. An attributed statement, so the FCDO's own page suffices if Andy wants it.
